attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post.

semantics.note: Keeps the 'entirely different tune' contrast, 'at every turn', 'effectively' and the claim that he is no longer talking about regulation. A retrospective observation.

contract.note: Pinning the claim to the May 8, 2025 hearing is reasonable. Splitting the shift from the universal 'at every turn' is a fair plain reading. The result depends on whether 'at every turn' is taken literally or as rhetoric.

evidence.note: Official 2023 transcript showing Altman backed an agency and licensing. This sets the baseline for comparison.
Official May 8, 2025 transcript: Altman called a prior-approval regime disastrous. That is opposition to the kind of licensing he backed in 2023.
Same hearing: Altman agreed a risk-based approach is the best way to set necessary guardrails. That is an explicit endorsement of regulatory safeguards.

reviews.rationale: The shift holds: in 2023 Altman backed licensing and an agency, and on May 8, 2025 he called prior-approval regulation disastrous. The stronger part fails: at the same hearing he endorsed risk-based guardrails, which meets the contract's contradiction condition for 'at every turn' and 'no longer talking about AI regulation'.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Limiting 'what was discussed' to regulation proposals fits the context, and the May 2023 to May 2025 window is right.

contract.note: Reading 'almost none' as 'only a small minority implemented' is fair and ordinary. The result depends on how proposals are listed and counted, which the speaker never specified.

evidence.note: Hearing transcript showing the range of proposals discussed (licensing, an agency, existing regulators). It does not show implementation.
CRS report, June 2025, before the evaluation date: no federal law created broad AI regulatory authority. This bears on some proposals but is no full inventory.
November 2024 launch of the international network of AI safety institutes. This is real international coordination, but voluntary rather than regulation.

reviews.rationale: The evidence suggests the headline proposals (licensing, a national agency) were not implemented. Some international coordination did happen. The packet has no proposal-by-proposal inventory, which the contract requires, and the packet itself says the result depends on counting choices. So the evidence does not establish 'almost none'.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Two-part observation: Congress passed no meaningful AI regulation, and Congress is trying to block state rules. The 'last hope' aside is rightly left unscored.

contract.note: Counting targeted laws that impose substantive duties on a specific AI harm as 'meaningful AI regulation' is an ordinary reading of 'any meaningful'. Assessing the two parts separately is fair.

evidence.note: Committee release dated April 28, 2025: the TAKE IT DOWN Act passed both chambers. It criminalises AI deepfake intimate images and requires platforms to remove them, before the post date.
California agency, May 13, 2025: describes an active House committee proposal for a 10-year moratorium on enforcing state AI laws.

reviews.rationale: The state part holds: a House committee was advancing a 10-year moratorium on enforcing state AI laws as of mid-May 2025. The 'failed to pass any meaningful AI regulation' part is contradicted under the contract's reading: both chambers passed the TAKE IT DOWN Act, which imposes substantive duties on AI-generated intimate imagery, before the post.

attribution.note: Marcus's own claim about OpenAI. He quotes Altman only to set up the contrast.

semantics.note: Keeps 'ever since', 'free training materials' and 'exemption from copyright laws', plus the contrast with Altman's statement.

contract.note: Reading 'exemption' as seeking fair-use protection for training, not blanket immunity, is a fair and ordinary reading given the training context. A literal blanket-immunity reading would be stretched against the speaker.

evidence.note: Official transcript confirms Altman said creators need to benefit. This establishes the premise of the contrast.
OpenAI's October 2023 Copyright Office filing argues training is fair use. Shows the advocacy began soon after the hearing.
OpenAI's January 2024 statement that training on public materials is fair use. Company statement used as evidence of its own advocacy.
OpenAI's March 2025 submission to the White House science office pushes fair-use access for training. Shows the position held into 2025.
Axel Springer licensing deal, December 2023. Qualifies the picture, but it is voluntary and does not change OpenAI's general fair-use position.

reviews.rationale: Altman did make the creator-benefit statement. OpenAI then argued steadily, in October 2023, January 2024 and March 2025, that training on copyrighted works is fair use and needs no general licence. Its publisher deals are voluntary and do not change that stance, so the contract's support condition is met.
